AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To determine the impact of a 'Hot Clinic' (HC) on emergency general surgery patient flow-through.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: HC is a four-bedded area coordinated by a specialist nurse. The HC consultant sees emergency patients referred from the emergency department, general practitioners or those in preceding 24 h considered suitable for interim discharge while awaiting investigations and HC reassessment.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENTS
AbstractText.content: All patients with acute abdominal pain were evaluated in three 4 week groups: before (group 1), 1 month (group 2) and 6 months after the HC was introduced (group 3). Interhospital transfers, intrahospital ward referrals and trauma patients were excluded.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTION
AbstractText.content: Introduction of consultant-led surgical HC every weekday afternoon.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Proportion of patients admitted under general surgeons, length of inpatient stay and the proportion of patients referred again within 3 months were investigated.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: 1409 patients were referred, of which 1061 met the inclusion criteria: 307 in group 1, 326 in group 2 and 428 in group 3. There was no difference in gender distribution (p=0.759). Inpatient admissions were significantly reduced (85.0% vs 78.2% vs 54.4%; p<0.001) and the inpatient duration of stay was significantly shorter after HC introduction (median (IQR) (95% CI) 63.8 (29.0-111.6) (51.8 to 72.8) hours vs 48.8 (21.7-101.2) (42.0 to 55.6) hours vs 47.7 (20.9-92.7) (42.8 to 56.9) hours; p=0.011).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Emergency general surgery HCs are associated with significant reductions in admission rates and inpatient bed occupancy. This service redesign has the potential to dramatically relieve pressure on acute surgical services.
